In the first half of the year, crypto startups raised $11.2 billion, all flowing into regulated, compliant tracks

In the first half of 2026, capital flows in the crypto industry’s primary market showed a highly concentrated compliance-driven pattern. Based on a review of publicly disclosed financings by the team of Irina Heaver, founder of Dubai crypto law firm NeosLegal, crypto startups raised a total of about $11.2 billion during the period, completing 377 rounds of funding. Under the统计 methodology used, nearly all disclosed capital went to enterprises that are regulated and have licensing mechanisms, rather than to early-stage, unlicensed experimental projects that had previously been seen as industry identifiers. Some practitioners interpret this outcome as a temporary shift in capital preference, and it has also sparked discussions about whether the industry’s commercial-model focus is moving.

At the level of core facts, funding is strongly concentrated in tracks that need licenses to operate at scale. Payments and stablecoins lead with about $3.7 billion, the predicted market with roughly $2.0 billion, and crypto exchanges and trading platforms with about $1.7 billion. The predicted market figure stands out: Kalshi completed around $1 billion in funding in May, with participants including Sequoia Capital, Morgan Stanley, Ark Invest, and a16z. Polymarket received approximately $600 million in support from the Intercontinental Exchange. Related statistics also show that the predicted market completed 34 rounds of funding cumulatively within six months, indicating sustained institutional interest. The investor roster further confirms how deeply traditional finance and market infrastructure are involved: BlackRock, Apollo, HSBC, BNP Paribas, Citadel, Goldman Sachs, Nasdaq, and others appear in the investment sequence of regulated crypto companies. Mastercard acquired the stablecoin payment company BVNK for about $1.8 billion. The Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund ADIA participated in Canton Network’s approximately $355 million institutional blockchain financing, and also appeared alongside a16z, Apollo, HSBC, and others.

In terms of logical breakdown, licenses are being repriced from “compliance costs” to “scarce, defensible assets.” One investor noted that code can be forked in a short time, but obtaining key-jurisdiction licenses or permits often takes 18 to 24 months and requires substantial investment; what investors are effectively buying is the time window that later entrants need to catch up. Another view emphasizes that this is not merely a trade driven by a regulatory narrative, but an entry threshold based on revenue logic: regulation is the ticket, and commercial sustainability is the core of the pricing. Even the research method has limitations—undisclosed rounds are counted as zero, so the $11.2 billion figure may underestimate actual activity; and half-year data is only a snapshot—only multiple consecutive half-years can more reliably describe structural changes.

The impact path on the crypto market can be observed through capital allocation, product forms, and participant segmentation. Primary-market resources concentrating in payments, stablecoins, licensed trading, and prediction markets can help accelerate the rollout of compliant infrastructure, clearing and settlement interfaces, and institutional-grade products. At the same time, if innovations in permissionless experimentation cannot connect with mainstream primary-market capital, they may rely more on community collaboration, token mechanisms, and self-sustaining liquidity cycles in the secondary market—so funding conditions at both ends may become even more differentiated. More importantly, institutional players and retail users do not necessarily move in the same direction. As noted by exchange executives, financing data reflects institutions chasing licenses, but a large volume of small, high-frequency user trading still occurs outside the funding narrative. Demand scenarios and risk preferences are segmented.

The editorial assessment is that the materials above are better understood as a staged portrait of primary-market preference rather than a final verdict on the entire crypto ecosystem. The factual portion is clear: fundraising on the order of $11.2 billion, 377 rounds, and disclosed capital concentrated in payments stablecoins, prediction markets, and licensed trading platforms—all supported by public statistics. Speculation should be kept restrained: “the end of the unlicensed era” is a strong judgment and still depends on factors such as the scale of undisclosed financing, the activity level of open-source and experimental ecosystems, and whether real retail usage can continue to validate on the other side. For founding teams, the choice of jurisdictions and the licensing pathway may rise from being a secondary consideration to becoming a variable in the business model. For market observers, what should be watched next is whether the structure in continuous statistics is stable, how well licensed companies bring products to market, and the quality of exits—rather than the total figure from a single snapshot.

content:
上半年加密创企融资112亿尽入持牌合规赛道

2026年上半年，加密行业一级市场资金流向呈现出高度集中的合规特征。据迪拜加密法律机构NeosLegal创始人Irina Heaver团队对公开披露融资的梳理，加密初创企业在该期间合计募集约112亿美元，共完成377轮融资。统计口径下，已披露资金几乎全部进入受监管、具备许可机制的企业，而非早期被视作行业标识的无许可实验型项目。这一结果被部分从业者解读为资本偏好的阶段性切换，也引发关于行业商业模式重心迁移的讨论。

核心事实层面，资金分布高度聚焦于需要牌照才能规模化运转的赛道。支付与稳定币以约37亿美元居首，预测市场约20亿美元，加密交易所与交易平台约17亿美元。预测市场尤为醒目：Kalshi在5月完成约10亿美元融资，参与方包括红杉资本、摩根士丹利、方舟投资与a16z等；Polymarket获得洲际交易所约6亿美元支持。相关统计还显示，预测市场在六个月内累计完成34轮融资，机构兴趣具有连续性。出资名单进一步印证传统金融与市场基础设施的介入程度，贝莱德、阿波罗、汇丰、法国巴黎银行、Citadel、高盛、纳斯达克等均出现在受监管加密公司的投资序列中；万事达卡以约18亿美元收购稳定币支付公司BVNK，阿布扎比主权财富基金ADIA参与Canton Network约3.55亿美元机构区块链融资，并与a16z、阿波罗、汇丰等共同现身。

逻辑拆解上，牌照正从“合规开支”被重新定价为“稀缺且具防御性的资产”。有投资人指出，代码可在短时间内被分叉，而获得关键司法辖区执照或通行证往往需要18至24个月并伴随高额投入，投资者实际购买的是后来者追赶所需的时间窗口。另有观点强调，这并非单纯的监管叙事交易，而是收益逻辑下的入场门槛：监管是门票，商业可持续性才是定价核心。研究方法本身也有边界——未披露轮次按零计入，112亿美元可能低估真实活跃度；半年数据只是快照，连续多个半年才能更稳妥地刻画结构变化。

对加密市场的影响路径，可从资本配置、产品形态与参与者分层观察。一级市场资源向支付、稳定币、持牌交易与预测市场集中，有助于合规基础设施、清算结算接口与机构级产品加速落地；与此同时，更依赖无许可实验的创新若难以对接主流一级资本，或将更多依靠社区协作、代币机制与二级流动性自我循环，两端资金条件可能进一步分化。更关键的是机构与散户并不必然同向：有交易所管理层指出，融资数据反映机构对牌照的追逐，但大量小额、高频的用户交易仍发生在筹资叙事之外的场所，需求场景与风险偏好存在分层。

编辑判断认为，上述材料更适合被理解为一级市场偏好的阶段性画像，而不是对整个加密生态的终局宣判。事实部分清晰：112亿美元量级、377轮融资，以及披露资金向支付稳定币、预测市场、持牌交易平台集中，均有公开统计支撑。推测部分则需克制——“无许可时代结束”属于强判断，仍取决于未披露融资规模、开源与实验生态的活跃度，以及散户真实使用能否在另一侧持续验证。对创始团队而言，司法管辖区选择与持牌路径可能从附属事项上升为商业模式变量；对市场观察者而言，后续应更关注连续统计中的结构是否稳固、牌照企业的产品落地与退出质量，而非单次总量本身。

Their main positions are placed in CME near-month and next-month futures contracts—in essence, they leverage the futures term structure.

【你以为ETH凉了，其实机构在偷偷布局】

很多人一看ETH从高点跌了60%多，就觉得这项目不行了。

真的吗？

上周以色列最大的银行Bank Leumi宣布，2027年起客户可以直接在银行App里买卖ETH。这是什么概念？以前机构想买ETH，得自己搞托管、找合规渠道，折腾一圈。现在直接像买股票一样，点点手指就能上手。

我再跟你说个反直觉的事： Dartmouth大学捐赠基金最近减了加密敞口，从表面看好像是机构在撤退。但你仔细看，他们减的是现货ETF，换句话说——他们在调整仓位结构，不是清仓离场。

ETH现在$ 1879，7天跌了不到2%，成交量低迷，市场在观望。这些信号说明什么？说明大多数人在等，等一个明确的方向，等别人先动。

但你发现没有？机构已经开始在做布局准备了——不是炒概念，是真的在搭基础设施。银行系统接入ETH，这是能把ETH从"散户赌具"变成"机构可配置资产"的关键一步。

所以落到投资决策上，我给你个实在的判断：现在的价格区间，值不值得你花时间研究它背后的应用生态？当然值得。但要不要一把梭？我的经验告诉我，不要。底部是一个区间，不是一个点。

ETH这波下跌是基本面的问题，还是市场情绪的问题？
